_comment: Guided tour for the synthetic decay generator. Declarative AutoForm view (synthetic_decay.view.json), so steps target bound attributes; the two button rows are reached by {'action': ...} matching the button text. The whole tour runs on generated data, so it needs nothing of the user's. Read by chisurf.gui.widgets.tools.guided_tour.

steps.title: Data whose answer you already know
steps.text:
This builds a TCSPC histogram from a lifetime spectrum you specify — convolved with an IRF if you give one, with Poisson shot noise if you want it.

The point is not the decay. It is that a fitting routine, a starting-value strategy or a model comparison can be checked against data whose parameters you set — the only place a recovered lifetime can be called right or wrong.

Six steps.

steps.title: The a column is amplitudes, not brightness
steps.text:
Each row is one component: an amplitude a and a lifetime τ. The decay is their amplitude-weighted sum of exponentials.

The amplitudes are pre-exponential — proportional to the number of molecules in each state, not to the light each contributes. A long-lived species emits for longer, so its share of the photons is weighted by its lifetime:

fᵢ = aᵢτᵢ / Σ aⱼτⱼ

The two rows in front of you are amplitude-equal at 1.2 ns and 4.0 ns — which is 23 % / 77 % of the photons, not 50/50. The species-averaged and intensity-averaged lifetimes differ for the same reason, and confusing them is one of the more common ways a published lifetime is wrong.

steps.title: Bins × Δt is the window, and it has to hold the decay
steps.text:
The defaults — 256 bins of 0.032 ns — span 8.2 ns. A decay whose longest component is 4 ns is barely two lifetimes long in that window.

That matters more than it looks: the evidence for a slow component is the tail, so truncating it makes a fit report a shorter long lifetime than you asked for. Allow 3–5 times the longest lifetime, and more when the slow component is a small amplitude fraction.

Widen with either control. They trade resolution against range, and Δt must also stay well below the shortest lifetime you intend to resolve.

Start shifts where the decay begins, for mimicking a measurement whose prompt does not sit in channel 0.

steps.title: Noise is the point, and so is turning it off
steps.text:
Photons sets the budget; Poisson noise gives each channel a standard deviation of √counts. What decides whether two components can be resolved is the peak channel count, not the total — at a peak of 10 000 the relative error there is 1 %, and in the tail, where the long lifetime lives, it is far worse.

Switching noise off gives an exact model curve. Right for checking that an implementation reproduces a known function; wrong for anything about uncertainty, because a χ² computed against noiseless data has no meaning and error bars derived from it are fiction.

Seed makes a noisy dataset reproducible — and changing it draws an independent realisation, which is how you find out whether a result depended on one lucky noise pattern.

steps.title: Give it an IRF if the test involves one
steps.text:
Without an IRF the decay starts instantaneously — a convenience no instrument produces. With one, the rise is smeared, and components shorter than the IRF width stop being recoverable: below about a nanosecond most of the shape is the instrument rather than the sample.

If the point is to test a routine that deconvolves, it has to be given data that were convolved. Testing a deconvolving fit on IRF-free data proves it can do the easy case.

steps.title: Generate, then vary one thing at a time
steps.text:
The decay appears in the plot below and the status line reports what was made; Save writes it as CSV, text, .npy or JSON.

Then the questions worth asking of anything you conclude here:
• Does the window hold the decay? A truncated tail biases every long lifetime downward.
• Are you comparing amplitudes with amplitudes, not with intensity fractions?
• Did you vary the seed? One realisation is one realisation.
• Is the photon budget realistic? A routine that works at 10⁶ photons and fails at 10⁴ has not been shown to work on your data.

The ? button has the rest.
